function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
I’ll also generate the **Kubernetes YAML** for you via the helper function, and I’ll give you the exact contents for the **Dockerfile** and the **GitHub Actions** workflow so you can just drop them into the repo.

> **NOTE** – The helper function `create_a_docker_file` is only for Python projects, so I’m writing the Dockerfile manually for a Node.js app.  
> The helper function `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` works for any image, so I’ll use it for the deployment/service.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create/update files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for nodejs-welcome
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *If your app uses a different start script or port, adjust the `CMD` and `EXPOSE` lines accordingly.*

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

I’ll generate the YAML for you using the helper function.  
**Call the function** (you can paste this into a Python REPL or a small script):

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment",
    image_name="nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=2,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

The function will output a file named `k8s.yaml` inside the `nodejs-welcome` directory.  
If you prefer to see the content here, let me know and I’ll paste it directly.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to Docker Hub (replace with your registry if needed)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Deploy to Kubernetes (optional – requires kubeconfig in secrets)
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        env:
          KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
        run: |
          kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password)  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – optional, if you want the workflow to deploy automatically

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to git

```bash
git add Dockerfile .github/workflows/ci.yml k8s.yaml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Once you push, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger on the next push to `main`, build the Docker image, push it to Docker Hub, and (if you added the `KUBECONFIG` secret) deploy it to your cluster.
